Existing adaptation methods mitigate memory overhead through rank truncation, base weight quantization, dynamic budget allocation, and activation reduction.
The standard approach to parameter efficiency is low-rank adaptation.
LoRA freezes the pre-trained model weights and injects trainable rank decomposition matrices into each layer of the Transformer architecture.
By constraining weight updates to low-rank matrices, LoRA removes optimizer states and gradients for base weights.
Compared to GPT-3 175B fine-tuned with Adam, LoRA can reduce the number of trainable parameters by 10,000 times and the GPU memory requirement by 3 times.
However, LoRA couples magnitude and directional updates.
To resolve this, Weight-Decomposed Low-Rank Adaptation decouples weights into magnitude and directional components.

DoRA decomposes the pre-trained weight into two components, magnitude and direction, for fine-tuning, specifically employing LoRA for directional updates to efficiently minimize the number of trainable parameters.
The proposed modification leads to a training memory reduction of approximately 24.4% in fine-tuning LLaMA and 12.4% in VL-BART.
While LoRA reduces optimizer overhead, frozen base weights still require substantial memory.
QLoRA addresses this by compressing base weights into 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4).
QLoRA reduces memory usage enough to finetune a 65B parameter model on a single 48GB GPU while preserving full 16-bit finetuning task performance.
Double Quantization saves an average of about 0.37 bits per parameter by quantizing the quantization constants.
However, QLoRA introduces inference latency because 4-bit base weights and 16-bit adapters cannot be merged directly into standard linear layers without dequantization overhead.
QA-LoRA introduces group-wise operators which increase the degree of freedom of low-bit quantization and decrease that of LoRA.
After fine-tuning, the LLM and auxiliary weights are naturally integrated into a quantized model without loss of accuracy.
Standard LoRA assigns uniform rank across all layers, ignoring layer sensitivity.
AdaLoRA parameterizes the incremental updates in the form of singular value decomposition.
AdaLoRA dynamically allocates the parameter budget among incremental matrices by manipulating the singular values based on a new importance metric.
When adapting models to long context windows, attention activations become the dominant memory bottleneck.
Shifted sparse attention splits context length into several groups and conducts attention in each group individually.
LoRA for context extension works well under the premise of trainable embedding and normalization.
LongLoRA can extend Llama2 7B to 100k context length and 70B model to 32k context length, on a single 8× A100 machine.

Several limitations govern these methods and the empirical literature.

First, memory savings measured on specific architectures and precisions cannot be assumed to generalize across arbitrary batch sizes, context lengths, or hardware configurations without empirical profiling.
For instance, while QLoRA reduces static weight memory, long sequences remain constrained by key-value activations and attention matrices.
Second, low-bit quantization requires specialized tensor cores for fast computation; without hardware support, runtime dequantization creates latency bottlenecks.
Finally, all verified claims were grounded against full-text sources for the six registered papers.
We note that provider metadata from Crossref and OpenAlex reported a minor title variation for DOI 10.48550/arxiv.2106.09685 (LoRA), resolved by verifying the official text.
All comparative findings reflect verified literature, whereas informal assertions remain strictly quarantined.
